title: The future, and what might have been
version: Published online 30 January 2018; Philosophical Studies 176 (2019), 505–532; DOI 10.1007/s11098-017-1026-y
locator: Coordinator primary HTML check: §1.1 truth clause; §2.1 lawmakers paragraph; §2.2 feasibility.
assumptions: Growing-block ontology; abstract ersatz timelines; feasible extensions share history and laws; selected supervaluational semantics for future claims; primitive non-Humean laws/lawmakers.
conclusion: Authors propose that past and present concrete things plus laws make future truths true; candidate lawmakers are left open but must constrain block growth. Feasible histories may diverge despite sharing present history and laws, making some future sentences indeterminate under their selected semantics.
proof_status: Conceptual framework selectively inspected; no formal proof audit or physical model reproduction.
dependencies: Briggs and Forbes, The Real Truth about the Unreal Future (2012), p. 298 as summarized/cited in §1.1
open_questions: What exact facts individuate lawmakers, and do equal classical causal-past field data fix them?
Can the feasible extension structure be supplied by a specified relativistic field model without adding a preferred global present?
relevance: Strong law-based growing-block rival directly tests whether future truth requires existing future events and whether same past fixes complete grounds.
limits: Coordinator cross-check scope is limited to passages named here; lane record provides broader worker reading disclosure. Selected sections only, not a complete audit. Authors explicitly do not defend growing block in this paper and say they do not provide a complete theory of each nomological-package element. No relativistic causal-past formalization or theorem equating past data with lawmakers. The 2012 source was not re-read; its publisher abstract remains the only source checked for it.

title: On Metaphysics’ Independence from Truthmaking. Or, Why Humean Supervenience is Compatible with the Growing Block Universe
version: Author manuscript headed ‘Forthcoming in Erkenntnis’; published as Erkenntnis 88 (2023), 1467–1480; DOI 10.1007/s10670-021-00411-y. Manuscript version accessed via PhilPapers archive; publisher record dates online publication 10 May 2021.
locator: Coordinator primary author-PDF check: §3 opening and §3.1 printed pp6–8, visible excerpt of §3.2.
assumptions: Targets Briggs and Forbes (2017) incompatibility argument. Distinguishes Humean supervenience, growing-block ontology, truthmaker maximalism, future truth-values, and revised/future-directed truthmaking. §3.3's Humean-law argument assumes a Best System-style non-governing account.
conclusion: Author argues Humean supervenience need not entail standard truthmaker maximalism; growing-block ontology does not entail weaker future-directed maximalism; and present truth-values for future contingents may be rejected. These are arguments, not established results of physics.
proof_status: Philosophical argument; selected full-text read, not independently validated and not a formal proof.
dependencies: Briggs and Forbes 2017, ‘The Growing-Block: Just One Thing After Another?’ (discussed, not separately audited in this task)
relevance: Direct objection to deriving maximalism or truthmaker demands from growing-block/Humean ontology; directly tests the conditional local-ground argument in PRELIMINARY.
limits: Coordinator cross-check scope is limited to passages named here; lane record provides broader worker reading disclosure. Direct local retrieval via curl failed DNS; PDF was readable through web extraction. No page-image/render check. Selected argument audit, not full citation-chain audit. Does not establish semantic compatibility as ontological equivalence, and does not refute conditional A+B+C if independently stipulated.
open_questions: Can Filomeno’s replies be combined with a bivalent, outcome-matching semantics while retaining a growing-block ontology, and what additional grounds would that require?

Does the proposed causal-past restriction exhaust all relevant present grounds in a concrete relativistic model, or can primitive powers, selection facts, or law facts vary across past-matching solutions?
Which independently motivated principle, if any, supports same-ground truth supervenience for future-contingent propositions without assuming truthmaker maximalism?
Can temporalized truthmaking ground a future proposition when its event obtains while leaving its present truth status unsettled, and which temporal index does the grounding claim require?

title: Open future, supervaluationism and the growing-block theory: a stage-theoretical account
version: Synthese 199(5–6), 14249–14266 (2021); online 11 November 2021; corrected publication 2022; DOI 10.1007/s11229-021-03419-7; PMCID PMC8581605
locator: Coordinator primary HTML check: D,T1–T3 and GB1–GB6 clauses, strong/weak tense repair, footnotes16–21 and27–30.
assumptions: Growing-block framework; stages are possible growth stages, domains expand along R, stage-history semantics; the paper adopts rather than defends the gappy supervaluationist treatment and does not offer a reductive account of stage-talk.
conclusion: Author argues that stage-theoretic interpretation of supervaluationism can express growing-block ontology and avoid the quantifier problem he attributes to Briggs and Forbes's fixed-timeline quantifier. The present report independently reconstructs the quantifier-parameter issue in a finite one-history model.
proof_status: Selected full-text inspection of the clauses and target sections; no complete proof audit and no independent reconstruction of the full Briggs–Forbes semantics.
dependencies: Thomason 1970 branching-time supervaluationist semantics (as used by Loss)
Briggs and Forbes 2012 growing-block supervaluationist account (as reconstructed and criticized by Loss, §3; not independently audited here)
open_questions: Does a branching stage semantics with a finite terminal branch preserve the intended growing-block axioms, or must only nonterminal stages be admitted?
How should domain-sensitive quantification and stage shifts be adapted to relativistic partial orders without a preferred global stage-history?
Which parts of Loss's diagnosis depend on the reconstructed Briggs–Forbes quantifier clauses, and how do they compare with the full original chapter?
relevance: Primary source for the exact frozen timeline / shifting stage domain problem and proposed repair.
limits: Coordinator cross-check scope is limited to passages named here; lane record provides broader worker reading disclosure. Toy model is a simplification, not a reproduction of every source clause. The semantic result does not establish ontology, truthmaking, bivalence/gaps, or relativistic application.
